Everything on this page runs real R in your browser. You will practice the same workflow as **Coding Assignment 4, Parts A and B**, plus a **one-sample** *t*-test from lecture A008: explore the data, check assumptions, run the test, and interpret the result.

::: {.callout-note}
## Assignment vs this activity

On DataHub, Assignment 4 uses brittlebush CSV files. Here we use Palmer Penguins so you can practice in the browser. In **Part A**, bill length is pre-filtered for you in step 2. **Part B** builds nest-mate pairs from `penguins_raw` and asks you to `mutate()` a delta column, just like Assignment 4. In **Part C**, the `penguins` table can still have missing `body_mass_g` — you will drop those rows with `!is.na()` before the one-sample test.

For a **one-sample** *t*-test with transformation when normality fails, see [Coding Activity 6](coding-06-check-assumptions.qmd). Part C here runs a directional one-sample test on data that already looks normal enough.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Choosing a *t*-test

| Design | Test | H₀ in words |
|--------|------|-------------|
| One group vs a hypothesized mean | One-sample *t*-test | True mean equals `mu` |
| Two **independent** groups | Welch two-sample *t*-test | True means are equal |
| Two measurements on the **same** unit (pair) | Paired *t*-test | True mean **difference** is zero |

Welch's two-sample test does **not** assume equal variances. Default `t.test()` is **two-sided**; you can set `alternative = "greater"` or `"less"` when the research question is directional — choose the tail **before** you look at the p-value.
:::

## Part A — Welch two-sample *t*-test

**Research question:** Is mean bill length different between Adelie and Chinstrap penguins?

### 4. Shapiro-Wilk per group

Run `shapiro.test()` on `bill_length_mm` separately for Adelie and Chinstrap in `two_group`. Save as `shapiro_adelie` and `shapiro_chinstrap`, and print both.


## Hint

Run `shapiro.test()` separately on each group's bill lengths. Subset with `$` and a logical condition.

Example:

``` r
shapiro.test(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl == 4])
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="shapiro_two_group"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
shapiro_adelie <- shapiro.test(two_group$bill_length_mm[two_group$species == "Adelie"])
shapiro_chinstrap <- shapiro.test(two_group$bill_length_mm[two_group$species == "Chinstrap"])
shapiro_adelie
shapiro_chinstrap
```

Both p-values are above 0.05 — normality within each group looks acceptable for a Welch *t*-test.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: shapiro_two_group
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!exists("shapiro_adelie", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) ||
    !exists("shapiro_chinstrap", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "Save both results as `shapiro_adelie` and `shapiro_chinstrap`.")
} else {
  sa <- get("shapiro_adelie", envir = .envir_result)
  sc <- get("shapiro_chinstrap", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!is.null(sa$p.value) && !is.null(sc$p.value) && sa$p.value > 0.05 && sc$p.value > 0.05) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Both Shapiro p-values > 0.05 — normality assumption looks met for each group.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Run Shapiro-Wilk on bill length separately for Adelie and Chinstrap.")
  }
}
```

### 7. One-tailed Welch *t*-test

**Directional question:** Are Chinstrap bills **longer** than Adelie bills?

Re-run the test with `alternative = "less"`. Adelie is the **first** factor level, so `"less"` tests whether Adelie mean &lt; Chinstrap mean (i.e., Chinstrap is longer). Save as `t_two_sample_one_tailed` and print it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## One-tailed vs two-tailed

When the effect goes in the direction you hypothesized, the one-tailed p-value is about **half** the two-tailed p-value. Assignment 4 uses two-sided tests unless a question says otherwise.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: t_one_tailed
t_two_sample_one_tailed <- 

```

:::: {.hint exercise="t_one_tailed"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Re-run the two-sample test with `alternative = "less"` (Adelie is the first factor level).

Functions: `t.test()`. Objects: `two_group`, `bill_length_mm`, `species`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="t_one_tailed"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
t_two_sample_one_tailed <- t.test(
  bill_length_mm ~ species,
  data = two_group,
  alternative = "less"
)
t_two_sample_one_tailed
```

One-tailed p is still ≪ 0.001 — Chinstrap bills are significantly longer.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: t_one_tailed
#| check: true

  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Set `alternative = \"less\"` (Adelie is the first level; Chinstrap-longer is a \"less\" test on Adelie vs Chinstrap).")
} else if (!exists("t_two_sample_one_tailed", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "Save as `t_two_sample_one_tailed`.")
} else {
  tt <- get("t_two_sample_one_tailed", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!is.null(tt$p.value) && tt$p.value < 0.001) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "One-tailed test confirms Chinstrap bills are longer.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Re-run with `alternative = \"less\"`.")
  }
}
```

### 8. Interpret the two-sample test

Using `t_two_sample`, decide whether Chinstrap mean bill length is **significantly longer** than Adelie (α = 0.05). Assign `chinstrap_longer <- TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: chinstrap_longer
chinstrap_longer <- 
```

:::: {.hint exercise="chinstrap_longer"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Compare `t_two_sample$p.value` to 0.05, then check which species had the larger mean in `t_two_sample$estimate`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="chinstrap_longer"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
chinstrap_longer <- TRUE
```

p ≪ 0.05 and the Chinstrap mean exceeds the Adelie mean by about 10 mm.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: chinstrap_longer
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!exists("t_two_sample", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "Run the two-sample test first (exercise 6).")
} else if (!grepl("chinstrap_longer\\s*<-\\s*(TRUE|FALSE)", code)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Assign `chinstrap_longer <- TRUE` or `FALSE`.")
} else {
  tt <- get("t_two_sample", envir = .envir_result)
  est <- tt$estimate
  chinstrap_higher <- length(est) >= 2 && unname(est[2]) > unname(est[1])
  expected <- !is.null(tt$p.value) && tt$p.value < 0.05 && chinstrap_higher
  user_val <- grepl("chinstrap_longer\\s*<-\\s*TRUE", code)
  if (user_val == expected) {
    if (expected) {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Correct — reject H₀; Chinstrap mean bill length exceeds Adelie.")
    } else {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Correct — the evidence does not support that conclusion.")
    }
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Re-read the p-value and sample means in `t_two_sample`.")
  }
}
```

## Part B — Paired *t*-test

**Research question:** Within Adelie breeding pairs, is male body mass different from female body mass?

The raw Palmer Penguins file (`penguins_raw`) records individual birds with nest IDs like `N1A1`. You will build **72 Adelie nest-mate pairs** — one male and one female measured at the same nest in the same breeding season — then add a paired-difference column before running the test.

### 9. Build Adelie nest-mate pairs

From `penguins_raw`, keep Adelie penguins with non-missing body mass and sex — after `make.names()`, use `!is.na(Body.Mass..g.)` in `filter()`. Extract nest ID and year, keep nests with exactly two birds, then `pivot_wider()` so each row has `female_mass` and `male_mass`. Save as `adelie_pairs` (72 rows).

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: adelie_pairs
adelie_pairs <- penguins_raw |>

```

:::: {.hint exercise="adelie_pairs"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Objects: `penguins_raw`. Functions you'll likely need: `make.names()`, `mutate()`, `str_extract()`, `count()`, `filter()`, `inner_join()`, `pivot_wider()`, `transmute()`.

Workflow: extract nest ID from `Individual.ID`, keep Adelie birds with mass and sex, find nests with exactly two birds in the same year, then pivot sex to columns.

Small `pivot_wider()` example:

``` r
tibble(
  nest = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  sex = c("female", "male", "female", "male"),
  mass = c(3800, 3750, 3200, 3400)
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = mass)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="adelie_pairs"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
raw <- penguins_raw
names(raw) <- make.names(names(raw))
adelie_nests <- raw |>
  mutate(
    nest_id = str_extract(Individual.ID, "^N[0-9]+"),
    year = as.integer(format(Date.Egg, "%Y")),
    species_short = if_else(str_detect(Species, "Adelie"), "Adelie", "Other"),
    sex_l = tolower(Sex)
  ) |>
  filter(species_short == "Adelie", !is.na(Body.Mass..g.), sex_l %in% c("male", "female"))
two_bird_nests <- adelie_nests |>
  count(nest_id, year, name = "n_birds") |>
  filter(n_birds == 2) |>
  select(nest_id, year)
adelie_pairs <- adelie_nests |>
  inner_join(two_bird_nests, by = c("nest_id", "year")) |>
  select(nest_id, year, sex_l, mass = Body.Mass..g.) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex_l, values_from = mass) |>
  filter(!is.na(male), !is.na(female)) |>
  transmute(
    female_mass = female,
    male_mass = male
  )
adelie_pairs
```

72 rows — one nest-mate pair per row.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: adelie_pairs
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!exists("adelie_pairs", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "Save the paired table as `adelie_pairs`.")
} else {
  ap <- get("adelie_pairs", envir = .envir_result)
  if (is.data.frame(ap) && nrow(ap) == 72 &&
      all(c("female_mass", "male_mass") %in% names(ap))) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "72 Adelie nest-mate pairs — one row per nest with female and male mass.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Build 72 rows with `female_mass` and `male_mass` from `penguins_raw` (see hint).")
  }
}
```

:::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: mass_delta
#| check: true

    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Paired difference column added — mean male − female ≈ 682 g.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Check the formula: `mass_delta = male_mass - female_mass`.")
  }
}
```

### 16. Interpret the paired test

Using `t_paired`, decide whether males are **significantly heavier** than females within Adelie breeding pairs (α = 0.05). Assign `males_heavier <- TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: males_heavier
males_heavier <- 
```

:::: {.hint exercise="males_heavier"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Check `t_paired$p.value` against 0.05 and compare the male and female means in `t_paired$estimate` (male column was first).
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="males_heavier"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
males_heavier <- TRUE
```

Mean male − female mass ≈ 682 g within pairs; p ≪ 0.05.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
#| exercise: males_heavier
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!exists("t_paired", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "Run the paired test first (exercise 13).")
} else if (!grepl("males_heavier\\s*<-\\s*(TRUE|FALSE)", code)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Assign `males_heavier <- TRUE` or `FALSE`.")
} else {
  tp <- get("t_paired", envir = .envir_result)
  est <- tp$estimate
  males_higher <- length(est) >= 2 && unname(est[1]) > unname(est[2])
  expected <- !is.null(tp$p.value) && tp$p.value < 0.05 && males_higher
  user_val <- grepl("males_heavier\\s*<-\\s*TRUE", code)
  if (user_val == expected) {
    if (expected) {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Correct — males are significantly heavier within Adelie breeding pairs.")
    } else {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Correct — the evidence does not support that conclusion.")
    }
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info", message = "Re-read the p-value and sample means in `t_paired`.")
  }
}
```

## 22. Recap — functions you practiced

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each function do?

| Function | Role |
|----------|------|
| `ggplot()` + `geom_boxplot()` | Compare a continuous variable across groups |
| `filter()` | Keep rows for the groups you want to compare |
| `pivot_wider()` | Reshape long nest records to one row per pair |
| `mutate()` | Compute paired difference (`mass_delta`) |
| `shapiro.test()` | Test normality (H₀: data are normal) |
| `t.test(x, mu = ..., alternative = "greater")` | One-sample *t*-test against a hypothesized mean |
| `t.test(y ~ x, data = ...)` | Welch two-sample *t*-test (default two-sided) |
| `t.test(..., alternative = "less")` | One-tailed Welch test |
| `ggplot()` + `geom_histogram()` | Visual check on one sample or paired differences |
| `t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)` | Paired *t*-test on two matched columns |
| `t.test(delta, mu = 0)` | Equivalent one-sample test on differences |

If you can explain each row, you have covered **Coding Assignment 4, Parts A and B** plus the lecture one-sample workflow.
:::

## Keep playing

What if you compare **Gentoo male vs female** body mass with a two-sample Welch test instead of a paired design? Load `penguins`, filter to Gentoo with complete sex and mass, and run `t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex, data = gentoo)`.

```{webr}
#| envir: ttests_lab
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
gentoo <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo", !is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(sex))
t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex, data = gentoo)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Same biological question (sex difference in mass), different experimental design — independent samples vs matched pairs. The test you choose follows from **how the data were collected**, not from what you wish were true.
:::
